prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A person's risk of stroke is associated with the number of fast-food restaurants near their residence, according to a study presented Thursday at a stroke conference in San Diego, California. Fast-food restaurants may be associated with stroke risk, a new study says. Some say there's not enough evidence. Researchers led by Dr. Lewis B. Morgenstern at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor counted 1,247 strokes caused by blood clots in 64 census tracts in Nueces County, Texas, which includes Corpus Christi, from January 2000 through June 2003. They also mapped the county's 262 fast-food restaurants and then adjusted for socioeconomic status and demographics and found a statistically significant association. "The association suggested that the risk of stroke in a neighborhood increased by 1 percent for every fast-food restaurant," the authors wrote in a poster presented at the American Stroke Association's International Stroke Conference. Residents of neighborhoods in the 75th percentile of fast-food restaurants had a 6 percent increased risk of stroke compared with residents of the 25th percentile of such eateries, according to the study, which was paid for by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. Morgenstern, director of the University of Michigan's stroke program and professor of neurology and epidemiology, warned that the finding does not prove that proximity to fast-food restaurants caused the increase in strokes of people living nearby.  Watch more on the link between fast food restaurants and stroke » . "What we don't know is whether fast food actually increased the risk because of its contents or whether fast-food restaurants are a marker of unhealthy neighborhoods," he said. Still, he added, "If this association is causal, the findings have large public health importance due to the high prevalence of fast-food restaurants." A spokeswoman for the National Restaurant Association lambasted that concern as unsupported by the data. "This article is seriously flawed and by its own admission shows no correlation whatsoever between dining at chain restaurants and incidence of stroke," Beth Johnson said. "Further, it tells us nothing about the eating and exercise habits of the individuals involved. The restaurant industry continues to offer a growing number of healthier offerings, move away from the use of trans fats and provide more nutrition information. "In fact, the National Restaurant Association strongly supports a national, uniform approach to providing detailed nutrition information in chain restaurants. Constructive and responsive measures like these, and not misleading studies, will help consumers make healthy choices for themselves and their families," she added.

(CNN) — A person’s risk of stroke may be associated with the number of fast-food restaurants near their home, according to a study presented Thursday at a stroke conference in San Diego, California.

A new study suggests that fast-food restaurants may be linked to stroke risk, though some observers say there is not enough evidence to support that conclusion.

Researchers led by Dr. Lewis B. Morgenstern of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor identified 1,247 strokes caused by blood clots across 64 census tracts in Nueces County, Texas, which includes Corpus Christi, between January 2000 and June 2003. They also mapped the county’s 262 fast-food restaurants. After adjusting for socioeconomic status and demographics, the researchers found a statistically significant association.

“The association suggested that the risk of stroke in a neighborhood increased by 1 percent for every fast-food restaurant,” the authors wrote in a poster presented at the American Stroke Association’s International Stroke Conference.

Residents of neighborhoods in the 75th percentile for the number of fast-food restaurants had a 6 percent higher risk of stroke compared with residents of neighborhoods in the 25th percentile, according to the study, which was funded by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.

Morgenstern, director of the University of Michigan’s stroke program and a professor of neurology and epidemiology, cautioned that the findings do not prove that proximity to fast-food restaurants caused the increase in strokes among people living nearby.

“What we don’t know is whether fast food actually increased the risk because of its contents or whether fast-food restaurants are a marker of unhealthy neighborhoods,” he said.

Still, he added, “If this association is causal, the findings have large public health importance due to the high prevalence of fast-food restaurants.”

A spokeswoman for the National Restaurant Association criticized that concern as unsupported by the data.

“This article is seriously flawed and by its own admission shows no correlation whatsoever between dining at chain restaurants and incidence of stroke,” Beth Johnson said. “Further, it tells us nothing about the eating and exercise habits of the individuals involved. The restaurant industry continues to offer a growing number of healthier offerings, move away from the use of trans fats and provide more nutrition information.

“In fact, the National Restaurant Association strongly supports a national, uniform approach to providing detailed nutrition information in chain restaurants. Constructive and responsive measures like these, and not misleading studies, will help consumers make healthy choices for themselves and their families,” she added.

A study conducted in Nueces County, Texas, investigated whether people living near fast-food restaurants faced a higher risk of stroke. Researchers focused on clot-related strokes, also known as ischemic strokes, which occur when blood flow to the brain is blocked. They mapped 1,247 ischemic stroke cases in the county and compared their locations with the locations of 262 fast-food restaurants.

To better understand the relationship, the researchers also accounted for other factors that can influence stroke risk. These included demographic characteristics, such as age and ethnicity, as well as socioeconomic conditions, such as income and neighborhood disadvantage. By adjusting for these factors, the study aimed to determine whether proximity to fast-food restaurants was associated with stroke risk beyond the effects of population makeup or economic conditions.

The analysis found a small but statistically significant association: stroke risk increased by about 1 percent for each fast-food restaurant located nearby. In other words, people living in areas with more fast-food restaurants appeared to have a slightly higher risk of ischemic stroke than those living in areas with fewer such restaurants.

The findings may have important public health implications. Fast-food restaurants are often linked to diets high in salt, fat, and calories, which can contribute to conditions such as high blood pressure, obesity, and diabetes—major risk factors for stroke. Neighborhoods with a high concentration of fast-food outlets may also have fewer healthy food options, making it harder for residents to maintain a nutritious diet.

However, the researchers emphasized that the study does not prove that fast-food restaurants directly cause strokes. The results show an association, not causation. Other factors not fully captured in the analysis, such as individual eating habits, access to medical care, physical activity, or long-term health conditions, could also help explain the relationship.

Even so, the study suggests that the local food environment may play a role in community health. If further research confirms these findings, public health officials and urban planners may need to consider how the placement and density of fast-food restaurants affect residents’ long-term health risks, including the risk of stroke.

# More fast-food restaurants near home may be linked to higher stroke risk, study suggests

Living in a neighborhood with more fast-food restaurants nearby may be associated with a higher risk of stroke, according to research presented at the American Stroke Association’s International Stroke Conference.

The study adds to growing evidence that a person’s food environment — the restaurants, stores and other food options available near where they live — may play a role in long-term cardiovascular health.

Researchers examined the relationship between residential proximity to fast-food restaurants and stroke incidence, finding that people who lived in areas with a higher density of fast-food outlets appeared to have a greater risk of stroke than those in neighborhoods with fewer such restaurants.

The findings were presented at a scientific meeting, which means they should be considered preliminary until published in a peer-reviewed journal.

## Food environment and stroke risk

Stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. It is a leading cause of death and disability in the United States and worldwide.

Well-established stroke risk factors include high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity, physical inactivity and poor diet. But researchers increasingly recognize that individual choices are shaped by neighborhood conditions, including access to healthy foods, walkable spaces and medical care.

Fast food is often high in sodium, saturated fat, added sugars and calories — nutrients associated with high blood pressure, weight gain and other conditions that raise stroke risk.

However, the new research does not prove that fast-food restaurants directly cause strokes. Instead, it shows an association: people living closer to more fast-food restaurants had higher stroke incidence.

## Why neighborhoods matter

Experts have long noted that health outcomes can vary dramatically from one ZIP code to another. Neighborhoods with many fast-food restaurants may also have fewer grocery stores, fewer safe places to exercise, higher poverty levels or more exposure to chronic stress — all of which can influence cardiovascular health.

That makes it difficult to separate the effect of fast-food availability from other social and economic factors.

Still, the study highlights the importance of looking beyond personal behavior alone, researchers said. Public health strategies aimed at reducing stroke may need to consider the broader environment in which people live.

## A reason for caution, not panic

The findings do not mean that living near a fast-food restaurant guarantees a person will have a stroke, nor do they suggest that an occasional fast-food meal is likely to cause one.

Rather, the research points to a possible population-level pattern: when less nutritious foods are more available and convenient, communities may face higher risks over time.

For individuals, stroke prevention still centers on managing blood pressure, not smoking, staying physically active, eating a heart-healthy diet, controlling diabetes and cholesterol, and seeking regular medical care.

A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish and lean proteins — and lower in sodium, processed foods and sugary drinks — is associated with better heart and brain health.

## What communities can do

The study may also have implications for city planning and public policy. Efforts to improve access to affordable, nutritious foods — such as supporting grocery stores, farmers markets, healthier restaurant options and nutrition assistance programs — could help reduce disparities in stroke risk.

Health experts say the findings are a reminder that preventing stroke is not only a matter of individual willpower. The places where people live, shop and eat may influence their risk in ways that accumulate over years.

More research will be needed to confirm the results and determine whether changing neighborhood food environments can directly reduce stroke incidence.

counterfactuals.output:
**Fast-food density tied to higher stroke risk in Corpus Christi study, but critics question conclusions**

A study of Corpus Christi-area neighborhoods suggests that residents living in census tracts with more fast-food restaurants may face a higher risk of blood-clot stroke, though researchers and industry representatives cautioned that the findings do not prove fast food causes strokes.

Researchers examined **1,247 ischemic strokes** — strokes caused by blocked blood vessels — among residents of the Corpus Christi area and mapped them against **262 fast-food restaurants** located across local census tracts. After accounting for neighborhood demographic and socioeconomic factors, they found that areas with the greatest concentration of fast-food outlets had a **statistically higher rate of ischemic stroke** than areas with fewer such restaurants.

The reported increase was modest: stroke risk was about **13 percent higher** in neighborhoods with the highest fast-food density compared with those with the lowest density. Researchers said the association remained after adjustment for factors such as age distribution, ethnicity and neighborhood income indicators.

The study was based on geographic patterns rather than individual eating habits. Investigators did not know whether stroke patients actually ate at nearby fast-food restaurants, how often they did so, or what other diet and lifestyle factors may have contributed to their risk. For that reason, the authors described the findings as evidence of an association — not proof of cause and effect.

Still, public health researchers said the results fit with broader concerns about neighborhood “food environments,” where access to inexpensive, high-calorie meals may influence diet, obesity, blood pressure, diabetes and other stroke risk factors. They also noted that fast-food density may be a marker for other neighborhood characteristics, such as traffic patterns, commercial zoning, walkability or access to healthier food options.

Restaurant industry representatives criticized the study, arguing that it unfairly singles out fast-food businesses without measuring what people actually ate or considering personal responsibility, exercise, smoking, family history and medical care. They also said many restaurants now offer lower-calorie or healthier menu options, and that locating restaurants in busier commercial areas could make them appear linked to health outcomes for reasons unrelated to food.

The findings add to a growing debate over whether neighborhood design and food availability contribute to chronic disease risk. Researchers said more detailed studies — including individual diet data, health histories and long-term follow-up — are needed before drawing firm conclusions or shaping policy based on fast-food restaurant counts alone.
